newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schaeuble sees chance for German tax deal - papers.
newsitem.headline: Schaeuble sees chance for German tax deal - papers.

text.p: Wolfgang Schaeuble, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's heir apparent and tax negotiator for Germany's Christian Democrats (CDU), said on Thursday he saw a chance to agree on tax reforms with opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
But, in newspaper interviews, Schaeuble said he would not allow coalition plans to cut 30 billion marks in taxes to be watered down in cross-party talks which resume on Friday.
"We want to make a big effort. But there will not be a result just for its own sake," Schaeuble told the Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung.

The top priority in the tax talks must be to fight record post-war unemployment. "Everything else is secondary. There can be no compromise that fails to serve that goal. That would just make things worse," he told the WAZ.

Schaeuble, who is also CDU parliamentary leader, struck a more positive note in a separate interview with the Die Woche weekly, saying both opposition and government must act together to fight joblessness. Dole queues hit 4.7 million in January.

"With unemployment so high, no party can afford to think only tactically. Whoever has been caught doing that was punished by the voters. That is why I see a chance to agree," Schaeuble told Die Woche.

Kohl and SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine held rare face-to-face talks on Monday to discuss a two-year package of income and corporate tax cuts drawn up by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to boost investment and job creation.
Waigel, Schaeuble and Hermann Otto Solms of coalition allies the Free Democrats (SPD) will meet a three-strong SPD team on Friday headed by parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping.

Schaeuble said he saw chances to reach agreement on cutting the main corporate tax rate to 35 from 47 percent, but there were problems with the SPD's opposition to a proposed cut in the top rate of income tax to 39 percent from 53.
Too big a split between income and corporate taxes would distort the tax system, open it up to manipulation, and be constitutionally dubious, he said.

The two sides have come together to try and strike an early deal which would bypass a stalemate in parliament -- where the SPD can block tax measures in the Bundesrat upper house -- and avert bickering from running into the 1998 election campaign.
Schaeuble told WAZ that agreement could also be reached on cutting labour overheads "as long as we do not lose sight of necessary reforms of the social security system".
But, he told Die Woche, there were fundamental differences of approach between the two sides to solving Germany's jobs and investment crisis.

"Does it make sense to use the prescription of John Maynard Keynes to try and stimulate consumption and investment? My answer is: No. If I have understood the leader of the SPD, he would tend to say: Yes," Schaeuble said.

Dismissing Lafontaine's answer, Schaeuble added: "Keynes' answer was developed for closed economies. They do not help in an era of global markets. Our jobs problem is a competitive problem. We have fallen behind in offering value for money."
Schaeuble, who has in the past made comments indicating he might be ready to consider a left-right grand coalition, ruled out such an option in the interview with Die Woche.
"The Social Democrats have said they don't want a grand coalition. We don't want one either," Schaeuble said.
